anti_patterns: Opening a channel for a single expected transfer: two on-chain transactions (open plus close) cost more than one direct on-chain payment.
Treating soft-finality as hard-finality: acting on an off-chain update as if it were settled before the challenge window on unilateral close has elapsed.
Ignoring the liveness requirement: going offline without a watchtower and expecting stale-state submission to be contestable.
Scaling participant count instead of topology: adding many parties to one unanimous-signing channel instead of using a channel network or hub.
Routing large payments over thin channels: attempting multi-hop transfers exceeding per-channel capacity instead of splitting or rebalancing.
Storing the only copy of the latest signed state on one device: losing it forfeits the ability to dispute.
Reusing a channel nonce: allowing replay of old signed states on a new channel with identical participants.
avoid_when: Only one or two on-chain-sized transfers are expected (open plus close costs exceed savings).
Participants cannot stay online or pay for a watchtower during the challenge window.
The interaction needs many parties to agree without unanimous signing.
Transfers routinely exceed what counterparties can lock as channel capacity.
Full public auditability of every intermediate update is required (intermediate states stay private until close).
Parties cannot agree on an adjudicator contract or challenge duration up front.
benefits: Instant zero-gas updates: once open, parties exchange fully-signed state versions peer-to-peer at network speed with no per-update transaction fees.
Minimal on-chain footprint: the happy path needs only two on-chain transactions (open and cooperative close) regardless of update count.
L1-grade safety given liveness: an honest party holding the latest fully-signed state always wins a dispute by submitting it within the challenge window.
General computation, not just payments: generalized state channels carry arbitrary contract storage plus balances, so game moves or contract calls settle off-chain.
Privacy of intermediate states: only the final outcome is posted on-chain in the cooperative case.
Unilateral exit without counterparty cooperation: any party can force closure with its latest signed state, so funds cannot be held hostage.
best_practices: Set the challenge duration to balance exit speed against monitoring burden (days, not minutes, for significant balances).
Run or rent a watchtower before opening any channel you cannot personally monitor around the clock.
Keep redundant, versioned copies of every signed state you countersign; the latest one is your dispute evidence.
Verify the adjudicator contract code and channel parameters (participants, nonce, challenge duration) before depositing.
Prefer cooperative close whenever possible: it settles in one transaction with no challenge delay.
Cap locked funds per channel and splice or rebalance rather than over-concentrating liquidity.
Use channel networks or virtual channels for multi-hop reach instead of widening a single channel to many signers.
Agree off-chain on fee handling for unilateral-close gas before disputes make it contentious.
component_types: Adjudicator Contract: on-chain contract holding deposits, verifying unanimous signatures, enforcing the challenge window, and releasing final payouts.
Channel Client: off-chain software per participant that signs, exchanges, and stores versioned state updates and submits open/close/dispute transactions.
Funding Module: locks participant deposits at open and supports top-ups or withdrawals without closing where implemented.
Dispute Registry: on-chain record of the highest submitted state version and challenge deadline during unilateral close.
Watchtower: delegated monitor that watches for stale-state submission and counters with the latest signed state before the deadline.
Channel Network Router: optional multi-hop layer (e.g. hash-locked routing over Lightning-style networks) connecting pairwise channels.
context: Two or more known parties expect a high frequency of small transfers or rapid contract interactions (micropayments, gaming moves, streaming money, IoT device settlement) where L1 throughput (~7-30 TPS on major chains) and per-transaction gas make on-chain execution infeasible. They can lock funds in an on-chain adjudicator contract up front, transact off-chain by exchanging unanimously signed, nonce-ordered state versions, and settle only the final outcome on-chain, with a challenge window letting any honest holder of the latest signed state defeat a stale submission.
design_principles: Unanimous Signed Versions: no state is valid without every participant's signature, so the latest held state is unilaterally enforceable.
Newest Version Wins: monotonically increasing nonces or turn numbers give the adjudicator a total order for superseding stale submissions.
Optimistic Happy Path, Adjudicated Sad Path: cooperative close is instant; the chain intervenes only on dispute.
Liveness as a Security Assumption: safety holds only if someone honest watches the chain during the challenge window.
Minimal On-Chain Footprint: intermediate updates never touch the chain; only open, close, and disputes do.
Fixed Capacity at Funding: channel value is bounded by locked deposits; design funding and rebalancing around that ceiling.
name: state-channel
tradeoffs: Liquidity lockup: funds committed at open are unusable elsewhere for the channel lifetime, with opportunity cost growing with duration.
Liveness burden: security depends on monitoring the chain during the challenge window, directly or via a paid/trusted watchtower.
Slow unilateral exits: disputed closes finalize only after the challenge window elapses, unlike instant cooperative closes.
Small fixed participant sets: every update needs all N signatures, so adding parties degrades liveness and risks stuck channels.
Bounded capacity: transfer size is capped by locked deposits; larger or bursty flows need splicing, rebalancing, or reopening.
Weaker guarantees than L1 consensus: a small participant set enforcing rules admits failure modes (stale submission, griefing) that mainnet consensus would reject.
Routing constraints in networks: multi-hop payments need path liquidity and add intermediary fees and griefing vectors.
use_cases: Micropayment streams between two parties (pay-per-use WiFi, content streaming, API metering).
Real-time gaming moves settled off-chain with only the final outcome posted on-chain.
IoT device-to-device settlement where devices minimize chain interaction.
High-frequency bilateral transfers (e.g. streaming salaries, per-second billing).
Off-chain execution of two-party smart contracts with on-chain fallback on dispute.
Virtual payment channels over intermediaries without per-payment intermediary involvement (Perun-style).
